title: They didn’t laugh.
paragraphs:
They didn’t laugh.
They didn’t argue.
They didn’t even look up.
They just rolled the dice.

Right there…
at the foot of the cross…
while Jesus Christ was bleeding above them.
Let that sink in.

The greatest moment in human history—
the redemption of sin,
the fulfillment of God’s eternal plan,
the sacrifice that would change eternity—
and the men closest to it were distracted by something small.

Not rebellion.
Not rage.
Indifference.
And that’s what makes this scene so unsettling.
Because it’s easier to recognize hatred than it is to recognize apathy.

Hatred pushes God away.
But indifference ignores Him completely.

The Roman soldiers saw Jesus as just another criminal.
Another body on a cross.
Another execution shift to get through.
So they did what soldiers often did—they divided His possessions.

John 19:23–24 tells us they took His garments and split them into shares.
But when they came to His seamless robe, they paused.

“Let’s not tear it,” they said.
“Let’s decide by lot who will get it.”
So they gambled.

Dice hitting dirt.
Coins shifting hands.
Eyes locked on fabric…
while the Son of God was giving His life a few feet away.

And in that moment—without realizing it—
they stepped directly into prophecy.
Psalm 22:18 had already declared it centuries before:

“They divide my garments among them
and cast lots for my clothing.”

What looked random…
was written.

What felt ordinary…
was ordained.

What seemed insignificant…
was prophetic.
And here is where the lesson cuts deep:
You can be physically close to Jesus and still spiritually blind to what He’s doing.
Those soldiers were closer to the cross than most people in history.

They heard His breathing.
They saw His wounds.
They stood in the shadow of redemption.
And still… they missed it.
Because proximity does not equal awareness.

You can sit in church every week…
hear Scripture…
say prayers…
and still miss the weight of what God is doing right in front of you.
That’s the danger of familiarity.

The cross was not hidden.
It was not distant.
It was not subtle.
But their hearts were elsewhere.

Focused on gain.
Focused on distraction.
Focused on something temporary…
while eternity was unfolding above them.
And if we’re honest—this still happens today.

We trade holy moments for trivial ones.
We exchange eternal focus for temporary distractions.
We fix our eyes on what we can gain…
and miss what God is giving.

The robe mattered to them.
But the cross should have changed everything.
And yet… they never looked up.
Here’s the powerful truth hidden inside this moment:
Even their indifference didn’t stop God’s plan.
Even their blindness didn’t delay prophecy.

Even their casual gambling…
was already written into the story of redemption.
God didn’t need their awareness to fulfill His Word.
And He still doesn’t.
That means something incredible:

Even when people misunderstand you…
God is still working.

Even when moments feel random…
God is still intentional.

Even when life feels chaotic…
God is still precise.

Nothing is wasted.
Nothing is accidental.
Nothing slips through His hands.
Not even the roll of dice at the foot of a cross.
But this story is not just about them.
It’s about us.

Because the question is no longer:
“Why did the soldiers cast lots?”
The real question is:
What are we focusing on while Jesus is calling for our attention?

What are we holding onto…
that is keeping us from looking up?
What distractions have quietly taken the place of reverence?

What moments are we treating casually…
that heaven considers sacred?
Because you don’t have to reject Jesus to miss Him.

Sometimes…
you just have to be distracted.

And maybe today is the moment to pause—
to lift your eyes—
to recognize what God is doing around you.
Because unlike those soldiers…
You still have time to look up.

“They divided my garments among them
and cast lots for my clothing.” — Psalm 22:18
“This happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled…” — John 19:24

Engagement Question:
If you’re honest—what’s one distraction in your life right now that might be keeping your focus off what truly matters?
